courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Quantitative Method: Survey and Unconventional Data Types
courses.description: The course focuses on the practical procedures of conducting sample surveys and analysis of complex survey data in social science research. The primary objective of the course is for students to understand modern techniques for design-based analysis of complex sample survey data. The course will first examine key steps in conducting survey research, from formation of research problem and hypothesis, sampling methods, questionnaire construction, types of data collection, handling of nonresponse and missing data, to data management, statistical analysis and inference, and interpretation of results. A secondary objective of the course is to introduce ‘unconventional’ data types in social science research, such as texts, social media and web data, and research strategies for analysis and visualization. The course emphasizes hands-on experiences with statistical software in data processing and analysis.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, you should:

* gain an understanding of common research procedures (appropriate level of details of various steps) and standards for good practices in survey research
* be capable of conducting research and analyze data (with a strong emphasis on research design, sampling strategy, and data collection)
* critically evaluate the work of other academics as well as the use of social science research in more popular outlets and arguments in general
* introduced to unconventional data types and their relevancy to social science research
* communicate skillfully, work effectively in groups, and improve project management skills

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Community Service-Based Learning for Sociology Students
courses.description:
Service-learning is a form of experiential learning in that students engage in cycle of service, knowledge application and reflection. This course provides Sociology students with an array of opportunities to engage in an immersive community service-learning experience. Working with community partners under the guidance of course instructor as well as mentors (in-service Sociology alumni teachers or community workers), students will complete specific projects and volunteer activities catered for specific learning needs of a student group in real-life setting, like teaching/tutoring/sharing knowledge, or designing a series of lessons particular topic on particular topic or problem the selected student group encountered.

Using the sociological imagination, students will identify the problem/ topic, gather information, design teaching/ learning objectives and outcomes, adopt appropriate delivering strategies, implement the plan with collaboration with their fellows and community partners. Upon completion of the practicum, students will put their sociological knowledge into dialogue with the experiential input from the service-learning setting, activities, and community partners through structured in-class discussions.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are able to:

1. consolidate and deepen the sociological knowledge they have acquired from the major curriculum in the course of teaching their secondary counterparts.
2. appreciate the value of serving the community and understand how sociological knowledge could contribute to the improvement of the community.
3. make use of effective collaborative learning process to advance information search and problem resolution.
4. cultivate empathic understanding of social needs of the disadvantaged groups in context and engage with outside partners to address social issues and develop social resolutions.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology of Education
courses.description: This course introduces to students the key theories, approaches, and ideas in the field of sociology of education. We will explore influential studies in sociology of education, and link them to educational challenges and problems in the real world. Education-related topics covered in this course will include stratification and inequality, school, family, peers, community, rural-urban divide, migration, gender, technology, mental health, mass education, and elite formation, among others. Through studying these topics, we will also discuss how education is connected to individual, community, and national development, such as whether education reduces poverty and promotes social mobility. Readings will not be region-specific but topic-based, covering empirical evidence across the world and representing the typical research questions on a particular topic. By reading and discussing empirical studies throughout the course, students will learn how to discover and analyze the key sociological and practical issues of education both locally and internationally.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Familiar with the most fundamental theories and concepts in sociology of education.

2. Know how to analyze educational issues from a sociological instead of personal perspective.

3. Understand the structural factors shaping and being shaped by educational outcomes.

4. Aware of the role of education (alleviating or exacerbating) in the worldwide social inequality.

5. Learn to evaluate empirical studies (both qualitative and quantitative) and think critically.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Movement
courses.description: This course enables students to analyze social movements and contentious politics through a sociological lens. The main objectives are to examine research in the sociology of contentious politics and reveal how sociological perspectives inform our understanding of state-society dynamics. Students will explore a broad spectrum of theoretical perspectives and research methods that sociologists use to study social movements. The course uses a 3-hour format that combines lectures, in-class discussions, and presentations. This approach helps students not only learn theories in the field but also complete a group project of their own interest with guidance from the course instructor.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing this course, students should be able to:

1. Identify key approaches in sociological research on social movements
2. Evaluate research paradigms and theories in social movement studies
3. Synthesize theoretical themes, conceptual perspectives, and empirical cases to conduct sociological research on social movements

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Cultural Sociology
courses.description:
The first part of this course introduces students to the diverse perspectives of cultural sociology. Both classical and contemporary approaches will be covered, from Karl Marx and Max Weber to the critical theorists and the postmodernists.
The second part of the course centres upon the empirical facets of culture, tackling such cultural issues and phenomena as subculture, high culture, popular culture, material culture, culture and the media, culture and power, as well as culture and ideology.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1

if !supportLists?1.endif?Understanding the nature and significance of culture in modern society.

if !supportLists?2.endif?Understanding the conceptual and research processes in the study of culture.

if !supportLists?3.endif?Understanding the major theoretical and critical stand points in the field of culture.

if !supportLists?4.endif?Developing skills in communication and articulation through intensive in-class discussion.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Religion in Modern Society
courses.description:
Many sociologists predicted that religion would gradually fade away in modern society and ‘modernity’ would eventually triumph over the ‘enchanted world’. On the contrary, the revival of traditional religions, blooming of new religious cults/sects, wide spread charismatic movement and fundamentalist movement of various sorts are taking place. Some contemporary sociologists therefore argued that we are in an age of ‘re-enchantment’ instead of ‘disenchanted’ modern society.

The course will be divided in two parts. In the first part, we will start from Max Weber’s theory to see how sociologists conceived the relation between religion and modernity as well as their conflicts. In the second part, we will go through contemporary issues concerning religious fundamentalism, religion and society in East Asia, China and Hong Kong.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken SOCI4352 or CURE3112.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Untitled Document 1. A general understanding of the major debates in sociology of religion.
2. A grasp of major issues concerning religion and society in contemporary world, with special references to China.
3. Through assignments and reading materials, students are expected to enhance (a) the ability to formulate meaningful research question; (b) demonstrate the ability to conduct your social research project, and ( c) enhance the ability to appreciate quality sociological articles/readings.
4. Study tours will be conducted to provide students with basic understanding and appreciation of artifacts related to religions, including buildings and their locations, images (and where people put them), icons (colors, size, postures, etc.), liturgy, paintings, in the perspectives of sociology of religion.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Science and Technology Studies
courses.description: What is science? What, if anything, is special about the way that scientists generate knowledge? And is scientific knowledge free of social influences? The first part of this course reviews how skeptical arguments from the philosophy of science (e.g., Popper and Kuhn) paved the way for the argument that scientific knowledge may be ‘socially constructed’. The second part provides an introduction to theory and empirical research in the growing field of science and technology studies (STS), which emphasize the social, cultural and contingent nature of scientific development.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Untitled Document

Familiarity with a range of influential recent and contemporary sociological ideas about the nature of scientific knowledge

Ability to assess critically theoretical arguments and their links with empirical evidence

Ability to make independent assessments of the comparative merits of rival accounts of the nature of science

Awareness of the role that science plays in contemporary society and the relationship between science and society

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology Internship: Nurturing Competency for Meeting Future Challenges
courses.description: Internship is a valuable educational experience that nurtures students’ competency for responding to challenges in the 21st Century. Integrating academic curriculum with supervised internship, this course provides students with the opportunity to make sense of real-life work experiences with the sociological imagination. Course seminars aim at two objectives: to advance students’ career preparedness with exposure to work, and to transform their sociological knowledge into sustainability skills that are essential for promoting organisational change for a sustainable future. Aside from gaining on-the-job skills, students will learn to apply sociological analysis to study their internship organisations in both private or public sectors. Utilizing critical thinking – a core feature of sociological training, students will identify and reflect on specific values, goals, workflow and structure, and social and environmental impacts of an organisation through their first-hand experiences in various professions. To successfully enrol this course, students must secure their local internship arrangement through obtaining approval from the field supervisor and the course instructor. Students must complete a minimum of 100 hours of supervised internship work aside from the regular course assignments and attending course seminars.
courses.learning_outcomes:
The course’s learning outcomes are built around: raising career awareness, applying sociology knowledge, developing sustainability skills and the ability to promote positive change in the workplace. Upon completing the course, students should be able to:

* Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of the internship organisation with the sociological imagination.
* Apply knowledge and methodological skills acquired in the sociology programme to real work environment.
* Outline the skills acquired from the job exposure and reflect on one’s competency.
* Appreciate one’s professional contributions to the internship organisation / related sector.
* Utilize sustainability skills to help address issues in the workplace or the community.
* Think critically about and explain how social factors shapes the workplace experience.
* Reflect on one’s value position and civic and workplace engagement.
* Identify ethical issues in a workplace and can make informed decisions on these issues.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Sociology and Modern Life
courses.description: This course explores key concepts, theories, and perspectives essential for sociological analysis. Students will develop a distinctive sociological imagination that differentiates sociological thinking from other disciplinary approaches. The course examines the relationship between individuals and social institutions throughout historical contexts, from early modernity to late modernity. Topics include sociological perspectives, self and social interaction, deviance, social stratification, work, urban life, global inequality, and environmental issues. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify major sociological perspectives, think sociologically, apply concepts to everyday social phenomena, and critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of sociological theories.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing this course, students should be able to:

1. Identify selected sociological perspectives and sociological key concepts.
2. Demonstrate the ability to think in a sociological way.
3. Apply different sociological perspectives/key concepts to social issues in everyday life
4. Evaluate the applicability of sociological theories by critically analyzing their strengths and limitations in explaining contemporary social phenomena.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Decoding Hong Kong Society
courses.description: In-depth analysis of selected issues and aspects of Hong Kong society from a sociological perspective. Topics discussion include Hong Kong’s business organization and economic development, social stratification and social mobility, political changes and conflict, urban development, culture, and family.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. After the course, students would have a good understanding of major trends in Hong Kong society.
2. Students would be equipped with the ability to analyze social issues with the aid of social theory.
3. Through guided tour and writing exercises, the ability to observe and research in social phenomenon will be cultivated.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Methods of Social Inquiry
courses.description:
This course provides a survey of the most commonly used methods, both qualitative and quantitative, in social research. It reviews the basic principles, procedures, objectives, and ethics of conducting social search. It introduces the common data collection and analysis methods, including survey, experiment, interview, observation, ethnography, big data, statistical analysis, causal inference, case study, content analysis, and process tracing. These methods will also be applied in group research projects. By taking this course, students will:

• understand what social research is and know the ethics of social research;• be familiar with the common social research methods;• know how to appreciate and evaluate existing social research; and
• practice social research and learn to present and write research findings.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Statistics for Social Research
courses.description: This course discusses the basic principles of statistical reasoning and their applications in social research. Basic techniques for descriptive and inferential analysis will be discussed to enhance students’ ability in analysing associations between social variables in the context of theory and hypothesis testing. Students will be given opportunities to use statistical software for analysing survey data. No prior computing experience is required.
courses.learning_outcomes:
The learning outcomes include:
(1) The role of quantitative evidence in scientific reasoning,
(2) Ability to articulate (verbally and in writing) the fundamental principles of statistical reasoning in relation to the role of quantitative evidence,
(3) Basic concepts and tools of statistics with special reference to the concept of spurious relationship and confounding bias, and
(4) Statistical literacy (ability to interpret the statistical results commonly reported in the mass media and applied social research, to recognize and avoid some common misuse of statistics).

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Theoretical Perspectives in Sociology
courses.description: The aim of this course is to familiarize the students with the theoretical traditions and development of the field of Sociology. Three focal areas will be covered to obtain a condensed overview of the major theoretical perspectives involved: 1) the contemporary relevance and revisions of the core Sociological traditions; 2) significant theoretical controversies and issues; 3) current attempts towards frameworks of theoretical integration.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Contemporary Chinese Society
courses.description:
The course will discuss the impetus of institutional change in contemporary China (1949 -) and its impacts on social and political lives of Chinese people. Key social science concepts such as
ideology, socialism, marketization, patron-clientelism, social control, civil society, industrialization, urbanization, class formation, social inequality, gender, family and special terms such as guanxi,
danwei, hukou, floating population, three-represents, harmonious society, China's dream. etc. will be introduced.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students should be able to understand the social science perspective used in this course to comprehend the main aspects of social change in contemporary China. They should be familiar with the key concepts and theories adopted from sociology and other social science disciplines in the analysis.

2. Students are expected to grasp the basic knowledge about China's major institutions such as socialist market economy, party-state politics, stratification and family etc.

3. Besides general knowledge, students are encouraged to focus on a special topic through their writing assignment such as the dilemmas between economic development and social equality, democracy and developmental state, traditional culture and modernization etc.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Globalization: Challenges and Responses
courses.description: Globalization has emerged as one of the most talked about concepts in the contemporary world. This course takes globalization as the master trend leading to profound changes in social life everywhere and will examine its multi-faceted manifestations in economic, political and cultural dimensions. Guided by the sociology of development, this course will seek to develop a broad interdisciplinary approach to the academic debates over globalization. Particular attention will also be paid to the challenges that globalization poses on human development and the responses that the global community has fashioned to tackle these challenges.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand the complex and multi-dimensional nature of globalization from sociological and multi-disciplinary approaches.
2. To comprehend the major academic debates arising from the process of globalization and locate current issues in the context of these debates.
3. To reflect on the impact of globalization on human development as well as the responses of the global community.
4. To master the skills in conducting analytical research on globalization issues.
5. To relate academic and community debates on globalization to our everyday life and formulate individual and collective strategies in responding to globalization and its impacts.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Social Problems and Inequalities
courses.description: Seemingly, citizens of modern society live with increasing affluence and liberty. Yet lurking behind prosperity and development is the widening of regional and social inequalities, the persistence of social exclusion and discrimination, and the emergence of new forms of social problems. Using insights from a variety of sociological theories, this course engages students in sociological debates about the meanings, patterns, causes, and consequences of these issues, and their impact on our lives.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Issues in Education and Society
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between education institution and the society. It offers a sociological perspective on social processes and outcomes of schooling. Topics such as major sociological theories on education, their application in analyzing the structure and processes of schooling as an organization and an institution, effects of education on societal level (the function of allocation and selection of education, credential system etc.) as well as the individual level (such as socialization and social stratification) are covered in the course. Empirical studies in Hong Kong, China as well as other societies will be adopted as illustration of theoretical analysis and application. Upon the completion of the course, students are expected to have basic understanding of sociology of education, and the capability to reflect on the meaning and significance of education and schooling experiences in a sociological way.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Special Topic in Sociology I
courses.description:
This apprenticeship-style seminar provides students with hands-on training in qualitative research methods through active engagement in ongoing research projects. Unlike conventional methods courses that emphasize theoretical foundations, this course treats qualitative research as a craft learned through supervised practice. Students will work collaboratively on faculty-led research examining contemporary social phenomena, gaining direct experience in research design, data collection, research ethics, analytical strategies, and scholarly writing.

The course is project-driven, and students will participate in all stages of qualitative inquiry—from conceptualizing research questions, designing research plans of data collection, conducting data coding and data analysis, to drafting manuscripts. Regular meetings combine methodological discussions, work-in-progress presentations, peer critique sessions, and individual consultations. Students will learn to navigate the ethical, practical, and intellectual challenges of qualitative research in real time, developing the judgment and improvisation skills essential to qualitative research.

By embedding methodological training within active research production, this course prepares students not only to consume qualitative scholarship critically but to produce it competently. Students will leave the course with tangible research outputs—such as analytical memos and draft manuscripts—that may contribute to their research projects or publications.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in MA Sociology
(1) The latest cumulated GPA (CGPA) scores must be 3.3 or above.
(2) Course instructor’s approval is required.
(3) Department add consent is required.
Note: The above requirements are not applicable to RPg students.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. **Design qualitative research projects**, including formulating research questions, developing research plans, identifying appropriate qualitative research methods, and preparing ethical review materials.
2. **Apply qualitative research methods competently in practice**, demonstrating effective qualitative research skills, and navigating practical challenges in data collection and data analysis.
3. **Analyze qualitative data systematically**, employing strategies such as coding, memo writing, and thematic analysis, while thoughtfully integrating AI tools where appropriate without compromising analytical rigor.
4. **Present qualitative research for scholarly audiences**, crafting clear, evidence-based arguments that integrate empirical materials with theoretical frameworks and engage critically with qualitative methodologies.
5. **Exercise critical reflexivity throughout the research process**, reflecting on methodological decisions, navigating ethical concerns (such as informed consent and confidentiality), examining researcher positionality and power dynamics, providing constructive feedback in collaborative settings, and contributing to collective knowledge production.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Health and Society
courses.description:
Health is a fundamental aspect of human existence and medicine is arguably the crown jewel of modern science. We all want good health, effective treatments of illness and affordable health care. Yet present-day health care is the flashpoint of many controversies: about the reliability of medical knowledge; and about inequalities in health and longevity. This course dissects these issues from a sociological perspective. We ask questions such as: What counts as illness? How do people understand illness? How does illness affect people’s life? Who gets ill and why? What is the role of medical technology in fostering health? Why do doctors and patients have trouble communicating?
This course surveys major approaches and areas in the sociological study of health, illness and medicine. The central idea is that we cannot understand the topics of health, illness and medicine simply by looking at the biological phenomena and medical knowledge, but instead, we must also consider a variety of social, political, economic, and cultural forces.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students are expected to learn to critically assess biomedicine from sociological perspectives.
2. Students are expected to gain understanding of sociological theories from empirical examples in health and medicine.
3. Students are expected to learn to draw links between their daily experience and observation, and conceptual issues.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: The Making of Modern Japan
courses.description: This course analyzes and delineates the sociohistroical invention and construction of seemingly distinctive "Japanese" institutions and cultural values shaped by various global forces in the historical process. Specifically, it attempts to depict a dynamic picture of how modern and contemporary Japan from the Meiji to the Heisei (1868-2018) period tried to respond to the idea of "modernity" and the "Western." Through a guided tour of Japan's experiences of the modern, the course shows both the enlightenment and despair brought by a series of political, social and cultural struggles for one to assert itself as a legitimate nation-state as seen from the eyes of others.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To adopt a sociological approach to understand and appreciate the social dynamics of the origins, arrangements and changes of various institutions in the Japanese society.
2. To analyze Japan by focusing not only on its national, ethnic or cultural-psychological attributes, as most frequently seen in popular discourses in Hong Kong or elsewhere, but also on the extent of global impact on the country's development.
3. To gain an in-depth knowledge of Japanese society, history and culture from both Western and Japanese sociological traditions.
4. To understand how both historical contexts and political power shape our sociological knowledge and research methods, especially our sociological inquiries of some major theoretical paradoxes of the Japanese society.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Doing Class in Everyday Life
courses.description: Although some theorists claim that ‘class is dead’ and thus fails to explain contemporary society, our daily life is still influenced by class factors, not only in terms of resource allocation but also in the ways we conduct our social life. In this course, we will explore how class shapes our lifestyles, housing, association patterns, life chances, education strategies, parent-child interaction, subjective identification and even political orientation. We do not simply take class as objective structural positions; we also perceive class as crucial social boundaries and distinctions that have to be practiced, performed and reproduced in various social fields. Such a perspective will help us to discover and reflect how our social life is ‘classed’.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Thesis Project
courses.description: This thesis project course provides students a hands-on opportunity to complete an individual research on a topic of interest under the instructor’s supervision. Students will be able to gain the firsthand experience in developing a research project and to consolidate their knowledge and skills in research methods. Through classroom trainings and individual consultations, the instructor will provide appropriate guidance to students during each stage of the research process and thesis writing.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing this course, students will have acquired in-depth knowledge on the topic relating to the current theoretical controversies, research issues, and methodological approaches in sociology. The specific course objectives include:

(1) To broaden the knowledge in a chosen field of study
(2) To analyze and integrate research literature in the field
(3) To apply the sociological perspective to the research project
(4) To strengthen research methods skills
(5) To complete a research report in an appropriate format

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Crime and Criminal Justice
courses.description:
The course explores relevant issues in the current conflicting society, particularly in the case of Hong Kong. Using relevant sociological theories and perspectives, students will be engaged in studying prevalent forms of criminal behavior and associated social issues, which have been brought about by rapid social changes.
Topics under discussion include the relationship between social development, social forces and crime, ranging from the traditional crime, such as drug abuse, to sophisticated commercial crime and internet crime, such as ‘distributed denial of service attack’, and transnational crime such as money laundering.
Social perception, responses and different approaches in the preventive strategies will also be reviewed.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing the course, the students should:
1. Have acquired a better knowledge on how criminological theories can help them to understand crime and social issues.
2. Have gained a deeper understanding of the social forces affecting crime and social justice in Hong Kong.
3. Be able to analyze crime and social justice issues theoretically and methodologically
4. Be able to apply sociological perspectives and insights to review, assess and construct measures against crime.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Organizational Design and Behavior
courses.description: This course introduces the concepts and theories for understanding the fundamental aspects of organizational design and behavior. A number of issues at the macro level, including organizational structure, external environment, corporate culture, organizational effectiveness will be considered. Major organizational processes, such as power and control, conflict, decision-making, innovation and change will be discussed. At the individual and group level, important topics like job attitudes, motivation, performance, and teamwork will also be covered.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:
1. grasp the major theoretical perspectives in organization studies
2. be familiar with current research in organizational theory and behavior
3. develop critical thinking and conceptual skills to analyze various organizational phenomena
4. be able to apply theories and models to workplace situations

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Advanced Theory
courses.description:
This course is primarily intended to give graduate students a detailed introduction to some foundational theoretical questions and positions in sociology. It is centered on the writings of Max Weber, Emile Durkheim, and Karl Marx, supplemented by other (and more recent) theoretical work. The readings and seminar discussions will cover three mains sets of issues: 1) the relationship between the individual and society; 2) the special challenges and problems confronting a science of society; and 3) theoretical accounts of key modern social structures. Secondarily, students will through a series of exercises leading up to a final paper gain practice in the essential skill of “reading and writing with theories.”

The course grade will be based on a term paper, which will be assigned a letter grade according to following rubric:
The “significant progress” mentioned in the rubric will be judged in reference to the writing exercises completed during the second half of the course but which will not be graded separately.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. to critically engage with different classical positions on how to conceptualize the connection between individuals and social relations or institutions
2. to confront the basic problems of what it means to have a science of society, and how this relates back to social life
3. to introduce students to the classic, and some more contemporary, interpretations of large-scale social transformations that characterize “modern” society
4. through a series of exercises leading up to a term paper, to train students in the essential skill of “reading and writing with theories”

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Advanced Methodology
courses.description: This is an intensive training course on the logic of theory construction and the logic of evidence building in empirical sociology. The theoretical and evidential logics provide the foundation for the effective use of qualitative and quantitative data analysis alike. The course will provide the tools for clarifying the theoretical and evidential logics of an empirical study and introduce three families of explanatory mechanisms that are relevant to diverse subfields of sociology. Most importantly, the course will develop the competence of students in theory construction and evidence building through learning-by-doing. Much of the course will be devoted to a re-examination of many exemplary works in empirical sociology from each theoretical family. The course will not focus on any philosophical debate or technique of data analysis.
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) Ability to (a) identify the logic of theory construction and the logic of evidence building of a publication in empirical sociology and (b) critically evaluate them, including the match between the theoretical logic and the evidence.
(2) Ability to apply the theoretical and empirical logics to clearly present an original research problem and a proposal to empirically study it.
(3) Practice in the formal presentation of empirical research results.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Advanced Statistical Analysis
courses.description: This course focuses on the causal modelling on different types of data. A major part of the discussion will be given to OLS regression in order to illustrate the modelling techniques needed for causal analysis. With this foundation, the lecture will move on to discuss the more sophisticated methods that require a deeper understanding of the statistical literature. Discussion will emphasize both the statistical reasoning underlying these methods and their empirical applications. At the end of the course, students should have sufficient exposure to a wide range of analytical methods, helping them to appreciate the quantitative research literature and to conduct their own empirical analyses.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Course Objectives:
(1) To understand the logic of statistical analysis
(2) To acquire skills on data management
(3) To evaluate the quality of a statistical report
(4) To perform statistical analysis

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.title: Advanced Qualitative Methods
courses.description: This course examines qualitative methods used in social science research. Since qualitative research is both an ‘analytic mentality’ and a set of practical skills, the course will focus both discussions of key methodological and empirical readings as well as on practical skills, such as case and informant selection, field experiences, interview techniques, writing field notes, and analyzing and writing qualitative data. The course is in a seminar format. Lectures will be interwoven with discussions. Students are also required to conduct a small-scale pilot qualitative research project using the skills discussed in the seminar.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students in this course should study and demonstrate understanding of the following: the discipline of sociology and its role in contributing to our understanding of social order and its changes; the role of theory in sociology; the role of evidence and qualitative methods in sociology; basics concepts in sociology and their fundamental theoretical interrelations; critical thinking; further develop transferable skills beyond disciplinary requirements; development of values, such that the student will see the utility of the sociological perspective as a useful and meaningful perspective on social reality and individual biography, for reflection of value positions and life choices.
